correctness.rationale: If \(\sigma(n)\) is odd, the standard parity criterion gives \(n=2^c m^2\) with odd \(m\). The pure two-power case reduces to \(2^{c+1}-1=3^b\), whose only nontrivial solution is \(c=1,b=1\). If an odd prime \(p^{2e}\) divides \(n\), multiplicativity forces \(1+p+\cdots+p^{2e}\) to be a power of three. For \(p\equiv0\) or \(2\pmod3\) that sum is not divisible by three; for \(p\equiv1\pmod3\), divisibility requires \(2e+1=3t\), and the factor \(p^{2t}+p^t+1\) has 3-adic valuation exactly one but is larger than three, so has another prime factor. A fresh divisor-sum sweep through 50,000 found only \(n=1,2\), corroborating the symbolic proof.
